title: The Blue Light
paragraphs: Once upon a time there was a soldier who had served the king faithfully for many years. But when the war ended, his many wounds meant he could serve no longer. The king said to him, “You may go home. I have no more need of you, and you will get no more money, because I pay wages only to those who do work for me.” The soldier had no idea how to earn a living. He left in great distress and walked all day, until toward evening he came to a forest. As darkness fell, he saw a light and made his way to it, and found a house where a witch lived. “Please give me a night’s lodging and a little food and drink,” he said to her, “or I’ll starve.” “Ha!” she answered. “Who gives anything to a runaway soldier? Still, I’ll be kind and take you in, if you’ll do what I want.” “What do you want?” asked the soldier. “That you dig up my whole garden for me tomorrow.” The soldier agreed, and the next day he worked with all his strength, but by evening he had not finished. “I can see you can do no more today,” said the witch, “but I’ll keep you another night. In return, tomorrow you must chop me a load of wood, and chop it small.” The soldier spent the whole day at it, and in the evening the witch suggested he stay one more night. “Tomorrow you’ll have only a very small job. Behind my house there’s an old dry well, and my light has fallen into it. It burns blue and never goes out, and you’re to bring it back up.” The next day the old woman led him to the well and lowered him down in a basket. He found the blue light and signaled for her to pull him up. She did pull him up, but when he was near the edge, she reached down her hand and tried to snatch the blue light from him. “No,” said he, seeing her wicked purpose. “I won’t hand over the light until I’m standing with both feet on the ground.” The witch flew into a rage, dropped him back into the well, and walked away.

The poor soldier landed on the damp ground without being hurt, and the blue light kept burning, but what good was that to him? He could see clearly that there was no escape from death. He sat for a while in deep sorrow. Then he suddenly reached into his pocket and found his tobacco pipe, still half full. “This will be my last pleasure,” he thought. He took it out, lit it at the blue light, and began to smoke. When the smoke had curled around the cavern, a little black dwarf suddenly stood before him and said, “Master, what are your orders?” “My orders?” said the soldier, completely astonished. “I must do everything you tell me,” said the little man. “Good,” said the soldier. “Then first of all, help me out of this well.” The little man took him by the hand and led him along an underground passage, and he did not forget to bring the blue light along. On the way the dwarf showed him the treasures the witch had gathered and hidden there, and the soldier took as much gold as he could carry. Once he was above ground, he said to the little man, “Now go and tie up the old witch and bring her before the judge.” Before long she came rushing past like the wind, riding a wild tomcat and screaming horribly. It was not long before the little man appeared again. “It is done,” he said. “The witch is already hanging on the gallows. What other orders does my master have?” asked the dwarf. “None at the moment,” answered the soldier. “You can go home, but be ready to come at once if I call you.” “All you need to do is light your pipe at the blue light, and I will appear before you right away.” With that he vanished from sight.

The soldier went back to the town he had come from. He took a room at the best inn, ordered himself fine clothes, and told the innkeeper to give him the finest room possible. When it was ready and the soldier had moved in, he called the little black manikin and said, “I served the king faithfully, but he dismissed me and left me to starve, and now I want revenge.” “What shall I do?” asked the little man. “Late tonight, when the king’s daughter is in bed, bring her here while she sleeps. She is going to work as my servant.” The manikin said, “That is easy for me to do, but very dangerous for you. If it’s found out, you’ll be in trouble.” When the clock struck twelve, the door flew open, and the manikin carried in the princess. “Aha! So you’re here!” cried the soldier. “Get to work right now! Fetch the broom and sweep the room.” When she had done that, he ordered her over to his chair, stretched out his feet, and said, “Pull off my boots.” Then he threw them in her face and made her pick them up again, clean them, and polish them. She did everything he told her without protest, in silence, with her eyes half shut. At the first crow of the rooster, the manikin carried her back to the royal palace and laid her in her bed.

The next morning, when the princess got up, she went to her father and told him she had had a very strange dream. “I was carried through the streets as fast as lightning,” she said, “and taken to a soldier’s room, where I had to wait on him like a maid. I swept his room, cleaned his boots, and did all sorts of lowly chores. It was only a dream, and yet I’m as tired as if I had really done it all.” “The dream may have been true,” said the king. “Here is my advice. Fill your pocket with peas and make a little hole in it. Then if you’re carried off again, the peas will fall out and leave a trail in the streets.” But the king didn’t see that the manikin was standing right beside him as he spoke, and heard every word. That night, when the sleeping princess was carried through the streets again, some peas did fall from her pocket, but they marked no trail, because the clever manikin had scattered peas in every street in town beforehand. And once more the princess was forced to do servant’s work until the rooster crowed.

The next morning the king sent his men out to look for the trail, but it was no use, because in every street poor children were sitting and picking up peas, saying, “It must have rained peas last night.” “We’ll have to think of something else,” said the king. “Keep your shoes on when you go to bed, and before you leave the place where you’re taken, hide one of them there. I’ll soon find a way to track it down.” The black manikin overheard this plan. That night, when the soldier again ordered him to bring the princess, he told the soldier about it. He said he knew no way to get around this trick, and that if the shoe were found in the soldier’s house, things would go badly for him. “Just do as I tell you,” answered the soldier. And so on this third night the princess again had to work like a servant, but before she left, she hid her shoe under the bed.

The next morning the king had the whole town searched for his daughter’s shoe. It was found at the soldier’s lodging. The soldier himself, who had gone outside the town gate at the dwarf’s urging, was soon brought back and thrown into prison. In his flight he had forgotten the two most valuable things he owned, the blue light and the gold, and had only a single ducat in his pocket. Now, weighed down with chains, he was standing at his dungeon window when he happened to see one of his old comrades go by. The soldier tapped on the windowpane, and when the man came over, he said to him, “Be so good as to fetch me the little bundle I left at the inn, and I’ll give you a ducat for it.” His comrade ran off and brought back what he wanted. As soon as the soldier was alone again, he lit his pipe and called the black manikin. “Don’t be afraid,” the manikin told his master. “Go wherever they take you and let them do what they like. Just take the blue light with you.” The next day the soldier was put on trial, and although he had done nothing evil, the judge sentenced him to death. As he was led out to die, he begged the king for one last favor. “What is it?” asked the king. “To smoke one more pipe on the way.” “You may smoke three,” the king answered, “but don’t imagine I will spare your life.” Then the soldier took out his pipe and lit it at the blue light, and as soon as a few curls of smoke had risen, the manikin was there with a small club in his hand. “What does my master command?” he asked. “Strike down that crooked judge and his constable, and don’t spare the king who has treated me so badly.” Then the manikin fell upon them like lightning, darting this way and that, and anyone his club so much as touched dropped to the ground and did not dare to move again. The king was terrified. He threw himself on the soldier’s mercy, and just to be allowed to live, he gave him his kingdom and his daughter as wife.
